_metadata.rubric: x01 expansion rubric (owner style examples, clicks-when-explained bar, explanation checked), 2026-10-18
_metadata.independence: I read only x01-b-review-input.json and no other file, search, web page or API.

hints.reason: Bowling: three strikes in a row is a turkey; Thanksgiving: the centrepiece bird. The bowling term turns an obvious word into a real 'oh, nice'.

best_available.why: Two solid routes, one of them a satisfying bit of sports jargon most U.S. players know.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent pair; nothing to change.

hints.reason: Layer: onions have layers; Shrek: the famous 'ogres are like onions' line, which itself is about layers.

best_available.why: A widely quoted movie line that ties both words in one breath.

pairs.pair_note: Strong pop-culture pair; LAYER may also pull toward CAKE on some boards, which is fine.

hints.reason: Computer: microchip; salsa: chips and salsa. A clean double meaning.

best_available.why: Clean, immediate double meaning.

pairs.pair_note: Solid; CHIP may also tempt toward COOKIE or POTATO if those appear on the board.

hints.reason: Baseball: catcher's or fielder's mitt; oven: oven mitt. Two everyday compounds; the 'catches hot trays' line is a nice touch.

best_available.why: Both compounds are everyday U.S. phrases.

pairs.pair_note: Clean pair.

hints.reason: Double: Double Dutch jump rope; oven: Dutch oven cookware. An unexpected word that clicks into two familiar compounds.

best_available.why: Surprising hint word that resolves neatly into two well-known phrases.

pairs.pair_note: Strong. 'Dutch oven' also has a juvenile slang meaning, but the hint itself and the explanation stay PG.

hints.reason: Bed: bedspread; jam: a spread for toast. Both senses are everyday.

best_available.why: Two common senses of one word.

pairs.pair_note: Fine; JAM side could also attract BUTTER or TOAST words on the board.

hints.reason: Bread: a loaf of bread; lazy: to loaf around. Noun/verb double meaning that lands well.

best_available.why: Neat noun/verb pun with no strain.

pairs.pair_note: Clean pair.

hints.reason: Kiss: 'pucker up'; lemon: sourness makes you pucker. Same physical action, two scenes.

best_available.why: Vivid shared action that works on both sides.

pairs.pair_note: Good; SOUR-type words on the board could compete for the lemon side.

hints.reason: Lemon: grated lemon zest; life: 'zest for life'. Both phrases are common.

best_available.why: Clean double meaning; arguably fresher than the obvious 'when life gives you lemons' route.

pairs.pair_note: Good pair; players may first think of the 'lemonade' proverb, but ZEST resolves cleanly.

hints.reason: Rome: Julius Caesar; salad: Caesar salad. The explanation correctly notes the salad is named after Caesar Cardini, which adds a fun fact.

best_available.why: Instant on both sides, and the explanation adds an accurate bonus fact.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent; the explanation is factually careful.

hints.reason: Cereal: a cereal bowl; football: the Super Bowl and college bowl games.

best_available.why: Two well-known uses; the Super Bowl makes the football side broad.

pairs.pair_note: Fine. The explanation's 'so does football's biggest game' works; naming the Super Bowl would be optional polish, not required.

hints.reason: Pit: peach pit (stone); princess: Princess Peach from Mario. Fruit plus pop culture is a satisfying combination.

best_available.why: Princess Peach is mainstream, and the pit side is literal.

pairs.pair_note: Strong pair; PIT could also pull toward CHERRY or OLIVE on some boards.

hints.reason: Pearl: boba are the tapioca 'pearls'; tea: boba tea / bubble tea. Close to naming the pearls directly, but not a plain synonym of PEARL in its usual (gem) sense.

best_available.why: The natural clue for this pair, now broadly known in the U.S.

pairs.pair_note: Judgement call: BOBA is very close to a context-specific synonym of PEARL; I accept it because PEARL's main meaning is the gem and the hint still has to point at both.

hints.reason: Cookie: fortune cookie; wheel: Wheel of Fortune (game show) or the wheel of fortune idiom.

best_available.why: Two of the most familiar phrases containing the word.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent pair.

hints.reason: Cake: molten chocolate cake; volcano: molten rock. Same idea as LAVA from the descriptive side.
Cake: lava cake; volcano: lava. The dessert name makes the volcano link feel playful rather than literal.

best_available.why: 'Lava cake' is the more common menu name, and the volcano side is the most direct possible.

pairs.pair_note: Both work; they are the same idea, so serve one. LAVA is slightly stronger and more fun.

hints.reason: Seed: sesame seeds; street: Sesame Street. A cheerful pairing of food and childhood TV.

best_available.why: Universally known show plus a common seed.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent pair.

hints.reason: Code: crack the code; nut: crack a nut (nutcracker). Common verb idioms on both sides.

best_available.why: Two everyday idioms using the same verb.

pairs.pair_note: Good; EGG or SAFE on the board could compete.

hints.reason: Bird: the swallow; throat: to swallow. Classic noun/verb double meaning, and the explanation's pun is charming.

best_available.why: Crisp double meaning with an 'oh, nice' turn.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent pair.

hints.reason: Tennis: the serve; waiter: serves food. Straightforward and fair.

best_available.why: Natural shared verb; the alliterative explanation is a nice touch.

pairs.pair_note: Clean; VOLLEYBALL on a board would compete for the tennis side.

hints.reason: Fork: pitchfork compound; tent: pitch a tent. The hint does not contain FORK and the compound is familiar.

best_available.why: A compound plus a verb idiom, both common.

pairs.pair_note: Good; BASEBALL or MUSIC words could pull PITCH elsewhere, which adds fair misdirection.

hints.reason: Football: the coach on the sidelines; stage: stagecoach. STAGE is cleverly read as half a compound rather than a theatre stage.

best_available.why: Misdirects STAGE toward theatre, then clicks as stagecoach.

pairs.pair_note: Strong pair with a nice twist.

hints.reason: Christmas Eve and New Year's Eve, a week apart on Dec 24 and Dec 31; the explanation is accurate.

best_available.why: The natural, exact link between the two holidays.

pairs.pair_note: Clean, if unsurprising; HOLIDAY-type words on the board could compete.

hints.reason: Arrow: Cupid's bow and arrow; valentine: Cupid is the Valentine's Day mascot.

best_available.why: The iconic figure who carries the arrow and stands for Valentine's Day.

pairs.pair_note: Solid pair.

hints.reason: Suitcase: cramming clothes in; test: cramming for an exam. Both are familiar scenes.

best_available.why: Relatable double scene with one verb.

pairs.pair_note: Good pair.

hints.reason: Mail: mail carrier; pigeon: carrier pigeon. Both compounds are common.

best_available.why: Two common compounds.

pairs.pair_note: Fine. The explanation loosely implies pigeons preceded mail trucks, which is broadly fair as history.

hints.reason: Mother: grandmother; piano: grand piano. The explanation says 'Grandma', which hides the GRAND + MOTHER compound it relies on.
hints.fix: Say the compound outright, e.g. 'Your grandmother might be the one playing the grand piano.'

best_available.why: Two familiar compounds; it just needs the explanation to name grandmother.

pairs.pair_note: Good; small wording fix only.

hints.reason: Canada: Canada goose; mother: Mother Goose nursery rhymes. A playful pairing of nature and storybooks.

best_available.why: Both phrases are household names in the U.S.

pairs.pair_note: Strong pair.

hints.reason: Bucket: bucket list; Santa: making a list and checking it twice.

best_available.why: A familiar compound plus a famous song line.

pairs.pair_note: Good pair.

hints.reason: Mosquito: itchy bites; wool: itchy sweaters. Relatable shared sensation.

best_available.why: Shared everyday experience on both sides.

pairs.pair_note: Fine; a word like POISON IVY or RASH on the board would compete.

hints.reason: Tornado: the twister carries Dorothy to Oz; curtain: 'pay no attention to the man behind the curtain'. Story-based route that clicks.

best_available.why: Two iconic scenes from one universally known film.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent pair; the curtain side is the delightful one.

hints.reason: Web: Charlotte's Web title and the spider's web; pig: Wilbur, the pig she saves. Accurate explanation.

best_available.why: A widely read children's classic that features both words centrally.

pairs.pair_note: Good; WEB is in the title, so it is the easier side, but the pig is the plot's heart.

hints.reason: Ninja: Raphael of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles; painting: the Renaissance painter Raphael.
Ninja: Leonardo, the blue-masked turtle; painting: Leonardo da Vinci and the Mona Lisa. Both facts in the explanation are correct.

best_available.why: Da Vinci is the most famous painter of the four namesakes, so the painting side is strongest.

pairs.pair_note: Same idea twice; serve one. LEONARDO edges RAPHAEL because the Mona Lisa makes the painting side instant.

hints.reason: Dog: Pluto, Mickey Mouse's dog; dwarf: Pluto's 2006 reclassification as a dwarf planet. DWARF misdirects toward Snow White, then clicks.

best_available.why: Cartoon plus astronomy, with good misdirection on DWARF.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent pair; 'most famous dwarf planet' is a fair claim.

hints.reason: Cabbage: cabbage patch (and Cabbage Patch Kids); pirate: eye patch. Two strong compounds.

best_available.why: Two iconic images joined by one word.

pairs.pair_note: Strong pair; PUMPKIN on the board could compete for the patch.

hints.reason: Wall: Humpty Dumpty sat on a wall; egg: he is almost always pictured as an egg. Half of a two-word name, but instantly recognisable as one word.

best_available.why: The nursery rhyme ties both words together immediately.

pairs.pair_note: Good. The rhyme never says he is an egg, but the egg image is universal and the explanation frames it as a scene, not a quoted fact.
